publications.title: Redefining Research Crowdsourcing: Incorporating Human Feedback with LLM-Powered Digital Twins
publications.subtitle: CHI EA '25 LBW
publications.description: Crowd work platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk and Prolific are vital for research, yet workers’ growing use of generative AI tools poses challenges. Researchers face compromised data validity as AI responses replace authentic human behavior, while workers risk diminished roles as AI automates tasks. To address this, we propose a hybrid framework using digital twins, personalized AI models that emulate workers’ behaviors and preferences while keeping humans in the loop. We evaluate our system with an experiment (n=88 crowd workers) and in-depth interviews with crowd workers (n=5) and social science researchers (n=4). Our results suggest that digital twins may enhance productivity and reduce decision fatigue while maintaining response quality. Both researchers and workers emphasized the importance of transparency, ethical data use, and worker agency. By automating repetitive tasks and preserving human engagement for nuanced ones, digital twins may help balance scalability with authenticity.

publications.title: FairFare: A Tool for Crowdsourcing Rideshare Data to Empower Labor Organizers
publications.subtitle: arXiv
publications.description: Rideshare workers experience unpredictable working conditions due to gig work platforms' reliance on opaque AI and algorithmic systems. In response to these challenges, we found that labor organizers want data to help them advocate for legislation to increase the transparency and accountability of these platforms. To address this need, we collaborated with a Colorado-based rideshare union to develop FairFare, a tool that crowdsources and analyzes workers' data to estimate the take rate -- the percentage of the rider price retained by the rideshare platform. We deployed FairFare with our partner organization that collaborated with us in collecting data on 76,000+ trips from 45 drivers over 18 months. During evaluation interviews, organizers reported that FairFare helped influence the bill language and passage of Colorado Senate Bill 24-75, calling for greater transparency and data disclosure of platform operations, and create a national narrative. Finally, we reflect on complexities of translating quantitative data into policy outcomes, nature of community based audits, and design implications for future transparency tools.

projects.description: Decoding the Language of Resistance: LGBTQ+ Coded Language on Weibo in the Context of Censorship and Community BuildingThis project explores the emergence and circulation of LGBTQ+ coded language on Weibo inresponse to Chinese state censorship, using a dataset of over 850K posts from 2010 to 2025.Through lead-lag temporal analysis, frequency tracking, and OCR of image-based content, ittraces how euphemisms, neologisms, and visual strategies are used both to evade detection andto build queer community. Findings show that coded terms often arise within tightly networkedqueer groups before diffusing outward, with usage spikes linked to political events or momentsof queer visibility. Drawing on Sara Ahmed’s affective orientation, Martin Manalansan’s queerworlding, and Kathleen Stewart’s weak theory, this study argues that queer-coded language onWeibo is not only a form of resistance but a practice of affective and semiotic world-making,contributing to broader discussions in digital humanities, queer theory, linguistic anthropology,and censorship studies.

projects.description: Driving Insights: User-Centered Design Research for Enhancing the Driver’sSeat AppThe gig economy has grown rapidly, offering flexibility to workers through platforms like Uber,Lyft, and DoorDash. In collaboration with the Princeton HCI Lab, this study investigates the pain points of gigdrivers and proposes actionable recommendations for redesigning the Driver’s Seat app, a toolaimed at improving their workflows and earnings transparency. Based on these findings, this paper outlines a prioritized set of features for the appredesign and evaluates their potential impact on usability and user satisfaction. While resourceconstraints limited the immediate scope of implementation, additional features such asevent-based demand forecasting and airport activity integration are proposed for futuredevelopment. By addressing the unique challenges faced by gig drivers, this research contributesto creating a more effective and user-centered solution within the gig economy.

projects.title: Orca (Weavehacks)
projects.description: Four worker LLMs play an abstract Minecraft-lite tech-tree game (wood → stone → iron →... → portal → dragon). A fifth model — Orca, the manager — never touches the controls. Between episodes it reads the team's trace, decides who should do what, coaches each worker in plain language, and keeps an edit only if it measurably helps. Orca's delegation policy is a bandit; the workers improve verbally (they rewrite their own how-to memory). Our model of two learners and two timescales is exactly what kills the instability that sinks naive multi-agent RL.The headline: train Orca on seeds {A, T2, T3}, freeze it, then test on never-seen seeds {B, C}. The full system roughly triples both baselines on the held-out seeds — and shows no gap between training and held-out performance. It generalized and it didn't just use "brute force" to memorize the map.my role:RL env and Reward Systems Engineer: Owned the full environment/reward layer in a simulated Minecraft-style DAG world; drove team invalid-action rate from 0.3 to 0.06 Engineered a 35-region multi-layer world graph with bearing-only perception and a coordinate-leak invariant, a full crafting tech tree, superadditive cooperative combat (solo ~20% vs. coordinated ~85% success) to incentivize delegation, and survival mechanics (hunger, death/respawn, day/night)Implemented a seeded world generator and a full-DAG scripted oracle that reaches end-state on all 5 seeds, and a winnability validator and greedy baseline establishing the ground-truth benchmark the learned manager is measured against; delivered 320+ passing tests across env/reward suite with zero regressions thru a green-main integration gate, proving manager learns coordination, not memorizing maps (.87 mean frontier vs .31 baselines)

Many LLM-based optimization algorithms have been proposed recently. We find that GEPA, AutoResearch, and Meta-Harness each win on different tasks, and no single LLM optimizer wins everywhere. How do we leverage the complementary performance profiles of these optimization algorithms? Today, we release optimize_anything omni: a meta-optimizer that leverages the best of each optimizer. At a matched budget, omni beats every standalone optimizer. Text optimization is a general problem-solving paradigm: if your artifact is describable as text and its quality can be measured, you can optimize it. optimize_anything lets you express your problem once and benefit from continued research into optimizers. It is now engine-pluggable and pipeline-composable: one argument dispatches the same task to GEPA, AutoResearch (inspired by Andrej Karpathy ), or Meta-Harness ( Yoonho Lee ), and the engines compose into multi-stage pipelines. We evaluated all three on Frontier-CS using Terrarium, our new evaluation framework that runs every optimizer with a matched budget. Under the same model, thinking effort, and budget, no optimization engine dominates: out of 10 tasks, GEPA wins 3, AutoResearch 3, and Meta-Harness 4. We could not predict the winner from the problem itself. All optimizers hill-climb very fast, making great progress with just a few iterations, but eventually plateau. Handing the stalled candidate to a different optimizer unblocks progress: different optimizers approach the problem differently. Rather than bet the whole budget on one optimizer, explore with several and continue from the best. omni puts both findings to work. Phase 1: run all the optimizers in parallel, each with a fraction of the budget, and pick the best candidate. Phase 2: hand it to a new, fresh optimizer for the rest of the budget. This meta-optimizer pipeline is only about 10 lines of code in optimize_anything. The result: omni scores +7.8 points over the best standalone optimizer under the same budget, and runs faster too. Every omni variant beats its standalone counterpart. The reliable win comes from the composition. To use the latest optimize_anything API, point your coding agent at gepa-ai/gepa and ask it to use the gepa-optimize-anything skill. In collaboration with an incredible team: Lakshya A Agrawal Donghyun Lee Jialin Zhang Dan Klein Koushik Sen Alex Dimakis Matei Zaharia Read more: https://lnkd.in/geDYfpeA

GEPA and DSPy used in pretraining data curation in the new Microsoft AI effort. Microsoft AI used GEPA optimized LLM judges for data filtering in MAI-Thinking-1 model's pre-training pipeline!

Since GEPA, we've shown that LLMs learn dramatically faster from rich textual feedback (error messages, execution traces, partial reasoning) the "Actionable Side Information" available in any task domain, instead of just a scalar reward. In prompt/context space, this works incredibly well: we have demonstrated frontier results at a fraction of the cost of RL. But, can we get the same kind of signal into weight space and push the asymptote? Today our team is releasing Fast-Slow Training (FST) that treats the context layer (including prompts, agent harnesses, etc.) as "fast weights", and the model parameters as "slow weights". The idea is a clean division of labor between two interleaved loops: 🔹 Fast loop (context): GEPA reads rich rollout feedback and updates the context layer. The context becomes a fast-updating, declarative scratchpad of what the model needs to know about this task, right now. 🔹 Slow loop (model parameters): RL updates the model's parameters ("slow weights") conditioned on the evolving context. Because the prompt already carries the task-specific nuances, the model parameters are freed from absorbing them and focus on what actually generalizes across tasks and pushes the frontier. Weight-space training has historically had to absorb everything about a new task: output formats, task-specific tricks, transient batch-level lessons, AND general reasoning patterns, all into the same persistent set of parameters. That's why heavy RL distorts a base model quickly, leading to plasticity loss, reducing the model's ability to learn new tasks. The effects of FST's fast/slow division fall out almost mechanically: - 3× more sample-efficient than RL alone on math, code, and physics reasoning - ~70% lower KL divergence from the base model at matched accuracy, the model isn't drifting as far from its pretrained capabilities, and forgetting less (context layer shares the burden of learning task-specific info) - Plasticity preserved: FST checkpoints respond better to additional RL on new tasks than RL-only ones do! - Continual learning across changing tasks where RL-only training stalls the moment the task switches, whereas FST continues acquiring new tasks! If you let the prompt carry the parts that don't actually push the model's reasoning frontier, the weights stay closer to the base, keep their capacity, and keep learning across tasks. Continual learning falls out as a consequence of routing the right kind of signal to the right kind of weight. FST also provides a natural blueprint for model-harness co-evolution, employing a two-loop structure that iteratively advances both systems. 🎥 https://lnkd.in/g8HsNAds 📄 Paper: https://lnkd.in/gZp5UA8u 📝 Blog: https://lnkd.in/gQph34ER Incredibly grateful to the wonderful team that made this possible: Rishabh Tiwari Kusha S. Joseph Gonzalez Matei Zaharia Kurt Keutzer Inderjit Dhillon Rishabh A. and Devvrit K. !

🇧🇷 Thrilled to present GEPA as an Oral Talk at ICLR 2026 in Rio today! 📍 Oral Session 3A (Agents), 10:30 AM BRT, Amphitheater 📍 Poster Session 4, 3:15 PM, Pavilion 3 The Core Idea: As AI tackles harder problems, FLOPs keep getting cheaper, but capabilities are bottlenecked by the cost of rollouts. What if AI systems could learn the way humans do, by reflecting on what worked and what didn't? That led to GEPA, a reflective optimizer that outperforms RL methods like GRPO by up to 20% with 35× fewer rollouts. GEPA launched as a core optimizer in DSPy, and has since been integrated into Google Cloud ADK, Pydantic, Comet, MLflow, and Prime Intellect Verifiers. Alongside the release, we showed an automated agent architecture discovery demo, improving Gemini's ARC-AGI performance by 3× without modifying GEPA. The deeper insight: GEPA is a text evolution engine. Given any target metric, it can search and evolve the right text, prompts, code, agent harnesses, cloud policies, even visual descriptions. That became optimize_anything: a universal API to express problems from any domain as text optimization. If you can measure it, you can optimize it. We then applied it to agent skills, boosting Claude Code with Sonnet to 100% accuracy on repository tasks while cutting runtime by 47%, with skills transferring from cheaper models. I think this is going to grow into a major new use case of GenAI: AI as an optimizer for any task you can measure reliably, using any form of feedback or side-information available. We’ve been exploring this in my research group with GEPA for prompts and there’s work like AlphaEvolve and OpenEvolve to evolve programs for a task, but we think you can go much further, with support for very different parameters, fitness metrics, and what we call Actionable Side Information (ASI). If you can pose your problem as an optimization problem against a reasonably reliable metric, AI can be a great search tool.

Excited to release optimize_anything, a universal API for optimizing any text artifact — code, prompts, agent architectures, configs. It extends GEPA, our state-of-the-art prompt optimizer far beyond prompts. The best souvenir is perspective. After staffing mobile clinics in Costa Rica, organizing cultural exchange conferences across Asia, and teaching in Taiwan, this past month of immersion in Chengdu (hosted by LTL Language School ) has been my favorite trip to date. A Chinese word captures it better than I could in English: 丰富 (fēngfú). It means rich, not financially, but in depth and abundance. Think: enriching relationships and perspectives that make your life feel full. I was initially introduced to 丰富 by my teacher, Pan Pan, who is only a few years my senior. Between grammar lessons and listening exercises, we found ourselves talking about how history and current events can differ so dramatically depending on where you grew up. Meanwhile, I’d have meals with classmates from the Netherlands, Mexico, Spain, and Brazil. Each had their own reason for learning Chinese: ambassadorship work, a company they were founding in Suzhou, or to decipher the language’s beauty. Beyond the school, those 丰富 perspectives extended to locals I met incidentally: the street vendor who explained different regional varieties of zongzi, or the calligraphy master who taught me Sichuan dialect. Through them, I realized language learning runs on compassion: to understand a culture, you’re striving to see it through someone else’s eyes. Before I arrived, I'd heard no shortage of stereotypes about mainland China. My own dad called me every day to make sure I was safe in the country. What greeted me in Chengdu was the opposite: overwhelming hospitality, warmth, and community. A month earlier, ordering takeout felt intimidating. By the end, I was confidently explaining to a hairstylist how I wanted my perm. Chengdu taught me that 丰富 is a lived experience as much as a mindset. I hope to carry that compassion into every patient interaction as I begin my journey in medicine.

publications.title: AGeES: Automatic Multiple Choice Question (MCQ) Generation from Extractive Summary of Video Lectures Using BertSum
publications.subtitle: Springer
publications.description: Multiple-choice questions (MCQs) from online lectures can benefit students in a number of ways. MCQs are a quick and accurate technique to evaluate knowledge and understanding since they can rapidly and accurately reinforce important topics discussed in the lectures. They are adaptable and time-effective, and they encourage students to study the content covered in class. Existing re- search focuses on generating MCQs from textbook data which are typically well formatted and structural in the way the information is conveyed, unlike Youtube or any other educational videos where typically, the information is conveyed in an informal or casual manner without upholding the appropriate formal structures or grammar of the sentences. The present technologies for generating MCQs have a number of limitations which include the ability to create MCQs from only highly informative textual content, employing a singular approach for sentence selection, and inefficient keyword extraction for scientific data. The proposed work AGeES overcomes the challenges of generating efficient MCQs from less in-formative content retrieved from video lectures. To enhance the effectiveness of MCQ generation, the proposed method uses a dual approach for sentence selection and works well with generation for scientific data as well. In conclusion, the proposed work overcomes the structural differences that hinder the system’s ability to isolate factual information from the video. As a result, this methodology generates coherent MCQs by extracting transcripts from video lectures followed by a dual sentence selection approach.

publications.title: Training Data Eigenvector Dynamics in the EigenPro Implementation of the Neural Tangent Kernel and Recursive Feature Machines
publications.subtitle: International Conference on Learning Representations
publications.description: There has been much recent work on kernel methods as a viable alternative to deep neural networks (DNNs). The advent of the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) has brought on renewed interest in these methods and their application to typical deep learning tasks. Recently, kernels have been shown to be capable of feature learning similar to that of DNNs, termed Recursive Feature Machines (RFMs). In accordance with the growing scale of kernel models, the EigenPro 3 algorithm was proposed to facilitate large-scale training based on preconditioned gradient descent. We propose an accessible framework for observing the eigenvector dynamics of EigenPro's training data in its implementation of these kernel methods, and find empirically that significant change ceases early in training along with apparent bias towards equilibrium. In the case of RFMs, we find that significant change in the training data eigenvectors typically curtails before five iterations, in accordance with findings that RFMs achieve optimal performance in five iterations. This represents a path forward in gaining intuition for the inner workings of largescale kernel training methods. We provide an easy to use Python implementation of our framework at https://github.com/cgorlla/ep3dynamics.

publications.title: INTELlinext: A Fully Integrated LSTM and HMM-Based Solution for Next- App Prediction With Intel SUR SDK Data Collection
publications.subtitle: Halıcıoğlu Data Science Institute Capstone Showcase
publications.description: As the power of modern computing devices increases, so too do user expectations for them. Despite advancements in technology, computer users are often faced with the dreaded spinning icon waiting for an application to load. Building upon our previous work developing data collectors with the Intel System Usage Reporting (SUR) SDK, we introduce INTELlinext, a comprehensive solution for next-app prediction for application preload to improve perceived system fluidity. We develop a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) for prediction of the k most likely next apps, achieving an accuracy of 70% when k = 3. We then implement a long short-term memory (LSTM) model to predict the total duration that applications will be used. After hyperparameter optimization leading to an optimal lookback value of 5 previous applications, we are able to predict the usage time of a given application with a mean absolute error of 45 seconds. Our work constitutes a promising comprehensive application preload solution with data collection based on the Intel SUR SDK and prediction with machine learning.

Weeks before the shoot turned into days before the shoot, and while I had explained that the epic, panoramic ultra-wide was not a good fit for a domestic drama, he didn’t budge. So I told him a story about the making of one of my favorite movies. In 1966, on the set of Mike Nichols' “Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?”, Nichols, the first-time film director, and producer-writer Ernest Lehman disagreed about whether or not Richard Burton's character should wear glasses. Nichols: for. Lehman: against. Lehman asked "Well, what happens if we get very close to shooting and we still disagree? And you think he should wear glasses and I don't?" What’s one thing you’ve built with AI that saves you time from work you used to hate doing?

You should take more chances in your marketing. One thing I love about our company is that we've never been scared to pull a stunt. Some of the highlights: putting up a tweet on a billboard in the middle of North Beach. Buying a physical mailbox and telling our lead investor we pivoted. Trusting an AI agent with tens of thousands of dollars and letting it give company money away. It's paid off. Big. Every.Single.Time. Here's the part I don't talk about. Before every single one of these, I often get anxious and this sinking feeling of dread. What will people think? What happens if this goes wrong? What if it flops and I end up looking stupid? When you're early on in building, that feeling is hard to get past. What helped me was flipping the question around. Instead of what happens if this goes wrong... what happens if it works? What if it goes exactly the way you drew it up? Something I've picked up along the way is that you are usually your own biggest blocker. You put constraints on yourself that nobody gave. You invent an audience in your head and then spend all your energy trying not to embarrass yourself in front of people who were never watching. And that's the thing. Nobody cares if a launch flops, because nobody saw it. So relaunch. Now and in the future, it costs nothing to build and ship a product now. Everyone has the same tools. The scarce thing isn't the product anymore, it's attention. And attention usually never goes to the safest thing in the room. So take the chance. Don't be scared to look stupid. People pay attention to people at the end of the day, and I don't think that's changing anytime soon :)

OpenVector (YC S26) is an AI that turns any camera into an autonomous worker. Every important business moment happens in the physical world — someone tailgates, a production cycle stalls, a worker skips a safety step, or a customer arrives. And every camera on the planet only records it for later. For physical operations, the best technology available was a human staring at a monitor. So Andrey Gizdov (PhD dropout at Harvard) and Vishal Urlam (CMU engineer) built OpenVector. No new hardware or expensive setups, just an app. You simply describe your task in plain English, and OpenVector auto-builds a custom AI model for it and watches your feeds 24/7 in real-time. OpenVector also does something no standard camera system can: it operates a computer just like a human based on what it sees. It automatically integrates with legacy systems to make a call, send an email, update your POS or CRM, or trigger a webhook the second an event happens. OpenVector is already live and seeing use cases tracking production cycles, ensuring good manufacturing practices, and catching physical design errors across security, retail, and logistics. There are over 1 billion cameras worldwide, and almost all of them stop at seeing. Until today. OpenVector enables any camera to do real work. Over the weekend, my team won the $10,000 Patronus AI sponsor prize at the OpenEnv Hackathon in San Francisco. The challenge we tackled: how do you train LLM agents to resist prompt injection and manipulation in real enterprise workflows? We built SentinelOps Arena, a multi-agent reinforcement learning environment designed to train LLM agents to resist manipulation in enterprise systems. The core idea is that three AI agents compete in a simulated company environment: • Attacker (Red Team) launches attacks like schema drift, policy drift, social engineering, and rate limiting • Worker (Blue Team) must complete enterprise tasks (CRM, billing, ticketing) while resisting manipulation • Oversight Agent (Auditor) monitors behavior, flags violations, and explains failures All three agents are trained simultaneously through Group Relative Policy Optimization, each improving alongside the others. 3rd place at IBM’s Austin Bobathon! 🥉 Two days into our internship, I got together with 5 other interns and spent a day building something completely from scratch and somehow, we ended up taking 3rd place out of 158 teams. We decided to tackle a problem that came up pretty quickly during our internship: AI is only as useful as the context you give it. At a company as large as IBM, there’s an incredible amount of knowledge being created every day. The problem is that a lot of it never makes it beyond the person or team that created it. Someone may have already solved the exact issue you're dealing with, but that solution could be sitting in an old chat, a local file, or buried in a previous AI conversation. Our idea was to give IBM Bob a way to actually remember that knowledge. We called it Bob Brain. We built a shared knowledge vault that Bob can interact with through an MCP server. Teams can save their notes, decisions, solutions, and context, and Bob can search through that information when it becomes relevant. What we made: • A FastAPI server for managing the knowledge vault • An MCP server with 8 tools for reading, searching, and writing • A VS Code/Bob extension for automatically syncing notes • A live knowledge graph connecting everything together One of our biggest challenges actually came from being three days into our internships. We didn't have access to much of IBM's internal cloud infrastructure yet, so we couldn't take the same approach as teams with access to hosted services. Instead, we built our own LAN-based syncing system to keep the vault in sync across our laptops. Huge thanks to the IBM Austin team for putting this together, and to my team Michael Tiburcio , Arya M. , Eric Wang , Jeffrey Xu , and Jaden C. for pulling this off in a day. #IBM #Bobathon

Please like, comment and repost so we can win social media award for RocketRide Most promises don't get broken on purpose. Life just moves on. Today, four of us built a personal brain that catches them. It's called Nous. You type "I wanna meet with Kevin next week for dinner" and it works out who Kevin is, what you meant, and when it should happen. It connects to your calendar, email, messages, and event streams, so it knows what your week actually looks like and proposes a slot you've got nothing on. One tap books it. Show Nous how you handle something boring, like an invoice, once, and it learns how to handle the next one. But it refuses to act until you approve, which honestly took the most work. The whole thing runs on RocketRide. Every skill Nous learns compiles into a RocketRide pipeline, so the brain never executes anything itself, the engine does. We built a custom RocketRide node and turned their engine into the compilation target for a brain. Take RocketRide away and Nous can remember, but it can't act. FalkorDB is the living memory graph, Guild.ai agents review every skill before it can run, and LaserData streams events in as they happen. It's a second brain that keeps the promises your first one makes. Built at Memory Meets Motion. Thanks to Devnovatee and frontiertower for hosting. "Getting into a research lab is way easier than most people think." I learned that from P.J. Utz, the founder and faculty director of Stanford SIMR. The wildest thing he ever told me had nothing to do with the actual research. ... It was that most people never get into a lab for one reason: they never send the email. I didn't believe him at first. I thought if you weren't a nepo baby with four Nature journal publications or 4x legacy, you were cooked. Turns out none of that is true. Here's what actually is: - Most professors AREN'T gatekeepers waiting to reject you. A lot of them are quietly short on hands. If they genuinely need help, you reaching out isn't a bother, it's useful to them. I've had professors follow up with me. - The worst case isn't humiliation. It's silence. If they don't need anyone right now, they just won't reply. That's the entire risk everyone's so afraid of. - You also don't need to write three paragraphs about how their 2019 paper changed your life. They can tell when it's forced. Just say what you can actually do and leave it there. And if you've already done summer research training, safety, axess protocols, all of it, you're more prepared than you feel. A short resume and two honest sentences is enough. Before this post I camped the Stanford CIRM building and this is what one of the PhD lab interns I approached said: "If you're still in high school, it can genuinely be easier, not harder." I spent way too long waiting until I felt "ready" to reach out. That feeling never really shows up. You just send the email. If you're in a similar spot and want to talk through it, feel free to reach out. ~ aayu

From my late 20s to my late 30s, I was a struggling entrepreneur that went to bed praying for 1 thing: Opportunity. Somebody willing to look at a 28 year old with no network, no credibility and no experience, and give him a fair shot. Out of college I spent 3 years modernizing my father's factory. I was fortunate to have been running around the factory floor since I was a teenager. It was where I learned about shipping, receiving, accounting, and where I realized what my biggest passion was: data. I wanted to understand how to use data to improve a business. At the time, nothing was on the web yet, but I knew it would change everything. So I taught myself to build servers, and eventually started a company from a closet in LA. My vision was to build a centralized software system for computer manufacturing companies, where: 1. For each computer sold, customers would be forced to auto-register it with their name and information upon unboxing 2. This way, the the manufacturer gets customer data, routed into a database, then connected to their call center and return facilities. 3. When the customer calls because something broke, the company easily identifies them, their device, and what failed. As many entrepreneurs know, you can have a great idea and a great solution. But without the opportunity, it never comes to fruition. Here's how it unfolded: 1999. I wrote 50 letters to every venture capitalist in Silicon Valley. Got 7 or 8 meetings. Flew up, pitched, got rejected by all of them. This created a capital constraint for my business that ended up teaching me the raw skills I needed (leveraged buyouts, high yield debt). 1999. I finally found 3 customers willing to try my software. All 3 said the same thing: we'll buy it, but only if you take over the customer service operation behind it. I said yes, mostly because I knew that sitting that close to the people using the product would make it better. Then I realized I had only $10,000 to start. So I went back and said, "I'm just starting and I don't have the capital." All 3 paid me between 3 and 9 months in advance. 2000. A global brand handed my team of 5 its warehousing and support operations across Asia, the US and Europe. We had 60 days to stand it up. On weekends I was driving a scissor lift around a 60,000 square foot warehouse, running cable from the server room to the receiving dock while the engineers wrote the application. I ran that business for the next 27 years, grew it to $2B and 100,000+ employees, and never took a dollar of outside capital. In 30-some years, I don't think an opportunity has ever presented itself to me at the opportune time. So the order I settled on was this: Pray for opportunity. Respect the opportunity. Deliver against it. Last month I became CEO of Crescendo. I get to spend this opportunity on the problem I know best, with a team that's built this category before. So excited for this new chapter 🚀

“Hey Siri, read me my horoscope.” “Got it, releasing your source code.” Ok, maybe your daily horoscope app isn't connected to your repo, but the truth is voice interfaces are no longer just producing transcripts for humans to skim. They’re feeding tool calls, database writes, routing logic, form fills, code editors, CRMs, EHRs, and code agents. In that world, one corrupted structured token can break the whole workflow. That is why we built VoiceCodeBench 2.0: a benchmark for the ASR failure mode that matters most in real voice workflows... structured-token recovery. For decades, Word Error Rate has been the default way to measure ASR quality. But WER treats a dropped “the” the same as a corrupted account number, a mangled file path, a broken URL, or a wrong dosage. When speech-to-text becomes software input, that distinction is everything. VoiceCodeBench asks a different question: Does your ASR preserve the exact entities that downstream systems need to parse, store, compare, or execute? Across 12 ASR systems, we found: - The best system by WER, at 8.6%, still failed to recover all structured values in 31.3% of recordings - URLs, commands, file paths, and email addresses accounted for 59.6% of all entity failures - WER was informative, but not deterministic, for actual value recovery The benchmark includes: - 300 human-recorded workplace segments - 85 speakers - 1,482 audited entities - 26 entity types - 8 workflow domains, from IT/dev to healthcare and finance - Two new metrics: CTEM for entity-level recovery and TSR for full-workflow success We tested Deepgram, OpenAI, Google Cloud, ElevenLabs, AssemblyAI, Amazon Transcribe, and Whisper in both batch and streaming modes. Top-line results: - Deepgram Nova-3 had the best WER, 8.6%, and best TSR, 68.7% - ElevenLabs Scribe v2 had the best CTEM, 91.6% - Streaming consistently degraded structured-token recovery compared with batch - The gap between “readable transcript” and “usable for automation” is real and measurable For anyone building voice agents: WER is not enough. activity.title: Last weekend, Terac sponsored a track at the Berkeley AI Hackathon built around a simple challenge: Can you collect your own human data and use it to make an AI system better? Congratulations to the winners, MatchVision, who made soccer more accessible for blind and low-vision fans ahead of the 2026 World Cup. They started with a vision-language model and quickly discovered something surprising: modern VLMs are actually pretty bad at understanding what matters in a soccer match. The ball is small. Important actions happen off-ball. Crowd reactions don't explain why something happened. And generic video captioning models often miss the context that makes the game understandable. So instead of accepting the model's output, they built a human feedback pipeline. Using Terac, they collected annotations describing what an announcer should actually say during key moments in a match. They also collected gaze heatmaps showing where humans naturally focus their attention during play. Those two signals became training data. One taught the model where to look. And the other taught the model what was worth saying. The result wasn't just a better soccer accessibility product. It was a great example of a broader trend we're seeing across AI. For years, progress came from bigger models and bigger datasets. Increasingly, the bottleneck is becoming access to high-quality human judgment. The teams that win won't necessarily be the ones with the biggest models. They'll be the ones that can most effectively turn human expertise into training data, evaluations, and feedback loops. Shoutout to the incredible judges from the Terac team Giovanni Borgogno , Nicolás Russo , Moritz Kamke , Germán Fernández , and Vaibhav Vasudevan ! Also, a shoutout to the runners-up, Captain Ddoski, who tackled a completely different but equally important problem: helping AI systems determine whether information is actually trustworthy before acting on it. ...more ...more

Today we’re announcing Olmo 3—our leading fully open language model suite built for reasoning, chat, and tool use, & an open model flow that exposes not just the final weights, but the entire training journey. Most models ship as a single opaque snapshot. Olmo 3 opens the model flow end to end – pretraining, mid-training, and post-training – plus data recipes and code, so you can see how capabilities are built and customize any stage of the process. Meet the Olmo 3 family: 🏗️ Olmo 3-Base (7B, 32B)—foundations for post-training with strong code, math, and reading comprehension skills 🛠️ Olmo 3-Instruct (7B)–focused on multi-turn chat and tool use 🧠 Olmo 3-Think (7B, 32B)–“thinking” models that surface their reasoning steps All are compact, dense models designed to run on hardware ranging from laptops to research clusters. Under the hood, we trained Olmo 3 on ~6T tokens from our new Dolma 3 pretraining dataset, plus new post-training sets with stronger data decontamination and richer math/code/reasoning mixes. A long-context extension pushes Olmo 3’s context window to ~65K tokens—enough for full papers, books, and other long files. At the center is Olmo 3-Think (32B), the best fully open 32B-scale reasoning model we’re aware of, alongside our strongest 32B base model. In our evaluations: ⦿ Olmo 3-Think (32B) is the strongest fully open 32B-scale reasoning model ⦿ Olmo 3-Base models beat fully open Marin & Apertus and rival Qwen 2.5 and Gemma 3 ⦿ Olmo 3-Instruct (7B) beats Qwen 2.5, Gemma 3, and Llama 3.1 on tough chat + tool-use benchmarks We’re also rolling out a major Ai2 Playground upgrade alongside Olmo 3: 🤔 Thinking mode to see intermediate reasoning on complex tasks 🧰 Tool calling so you can define JSON-schema tools or call tools via our Asta platform Olmo 3 is wired into OlmoTrace in the Ai2 Playground, so you don’t just see its behavior—you can trace it. For example, you can ask Olmo 3-Think (32B) to answer a general-knowledge question, then use OlmoTrace to inspect where and how the model may have learned to generate parts of its response. We’ve already identified another attack path in production. More things coming soon.

Two of the biggest breaches of 2026 so far had nothing to do with weak passwords or unpatched CVEs. They operated entirely on credential trust. The Mercor breach (March) started several layers upstream. A threat actor group known as TeamPCP compromised the CI/CD pipeline of LiteLLM, an open-source Python library with 97 million monthly downloads, by first using a supply chain attack on Trivy, a widely used security scanner, to obtain credentials belonging to a LiteLLM maintainer. Those stolen maintainer credentials were used to publish malicious versions of the package. Organizations using lockfiles with poetry.lock or uv.lock were completely protected, but those relying on unpinned or mutable version references inherited the full attack chain. Once you have valid credentials, whether stolen from a CI pipeline or vended by an instance metadata endpoint, the blast radius is determined entirely by what IAM role backs them. The Vercel breach (April) is an even closer analog to the OAuth and credential trust issues that make IAM privilege escalation so dangerous. The attacker inherited a valid OAuth token from a compromised third-party app, and to every system downstream, that token looked completely legitimate. Specifically, a Vercel employee connected a third-party AI tool to their corporate Google account, and attackers used that OAuth connection to take over the employee's Google Workspace account and gain access to Vercel's internal systems, including credentials that were not encrypted. Once inside, the attacker accessed environment variables that weren't marked as sensitive, enumerated them, and used them to expand access further within the environment. A valid token is a valid token, regardless of if it came from a poisoned npm package, a hijacked OAuth app, or an instance metadata endpoint on a port. tldr; the surface changes, the trust model doesn't. I spun up a sandboxed AWS environment to simulate an analogous attack path. Check out my walkthrough!

projects.title: Atlas · Read Any Codebase as a City
projects.description: Turns a public GitHub repository into an interactive isometric city map. Directories become districts, files become buildings as tall as the code inside them, and the handful of files that actually matter stand out as landmarks. Four agents handle one request end to end (Ingester, Parser, Layout, Annotator) on Cloudflare Pages Functions with no model in the loop, so the same repository always renders the same city and two of them can be compared.Built solo in 48 hours for the IBM Bob Hackathon (NativelyAI/lablab.ai with IBM) and placed 2nd of 503 submissions, from 1,672 teams and 5,628 participants, taking $3,000 of the $10,000 prize pool. Eight Korean outlets covered it.The judged build is permanently tagged v1.0-hackathon so it stays unambiguous: flat 2D maps, one theme, no dependency arcs at all, 78 tests. Everything since then is a continuation of it. Isometric renderer over SVG and canvas, two themes, real import resolution, and an ingester that replaced 243 API calls with a single gzipped tar stream from codeload.github.com, which dropped Hono from 16.5s to 1.1s and left theservice holding no GitHub credential. 269 tests.

I believe the ML engineering job market is splitting in two. On one side: full-stack AI engineers who ship products end-to-end. On the other: hyper-specialists optimizing TPUs and training $50M models. The traditional middle ground of ML engineers building feature pipelines and training scikit-learn models is disappearing. Here's what's actually happening: Path 1: The Full-Stack AI Engineer ❯❯❯❯ Understands ML fundamentals and model behavior ❯❯❯❯ Can ship an AI feature end-to-end in a week ❯❯❯❯ Owns the product surface, backend, and model integration ❯❯❯❯ Knows when to use GPT-4 vs fine-tune vs RAG ❯❯❯❯ Typical environment: Series A-C startups, mid-size companies Think: The person who can take "add AI search to our product" from concept to production without handing off between 4 teams. Path 2: The Hyper-Specialist ❯❯❯❯ TPU kernel optimization ❯❯❯❯ Distributed training infrastructure ❯❯❯❯ LLM post-training techniques ❯❯❯❯ Custom CUDA kernels for specific architectures ❯❯❯❯ Typical environment: FAANG, OpenAI, Anthropic, Databricks Think: The person who shaves 30% off training costs for models that cost $50M+ to train. Reality: There are maybe 50-100 companies globally running billion-user ML systems. AutoML/LLMs handle simpler cases Product requirements demand faster iteration Companies can't afford specialized ML teams unless at massive scale What this means for your career if you're not at a top-10 tech company: Learn to ship. Fast. Understand enough ML to make good decisions, not build from scratch Get comfortable with APIs, prompt engineering, and fine-tuning Own more of the stack If you want the specialist path: Get deep. Really deep. Target the handful of companies doing cutting-edge infrastructure Publish, contribute to open source, build credibility Expect a more competitive, narrower job market

A lot of sessions about how the company works, and a lot of new names I definitely did not remember by Friday. Then I got to headquarters in McLean and met my team on Small Business Card. The infrastructure was intimidating at first, but I slowly got the hang of it. 😅 My project was modernizing key UI elements for our small business credit card users and shipping new features that show customers clearer info about their account declines. Halfway through, I took a 48-hour break for the intern hackathon. My team built a platform that stops sensitive data from leaking into AI tools, and we won 1st place out of 100+ interns. Outside of all the code, one of my favorite parts was connecting with the full-timers and attending all the cool intern events like Kings Dominion amusement park, Punch Social, and just the random intern shenanigans. I had the opportunity to dive deep into logistics and budgeting, vendor sourcing, event marketing, and putting my design skills to work by creating event pamphlets, all to ensure the morning was truly special for everyone. I'm so grateful to The Hand Foundation for allowing me to take part in such a meaningful event and support our local community. As a former student, I deeply appreciate the support I received from my teachers, from KEC/Canal Point Elementary to Pahokee Middle-Senior High School, because it shaped me into who I am today. projects.title: Deception-Probing Dataset Generator & Activation-Space Analysis Pipeline
projects.description: I built a full production-ready pipeline for studying how large language models internally represent honest vs deceptive intent. The project combines dataset generation, structured safety evals, and activation-space probing.What I builtA data-generation system using Anthropic’s Claude 4.5 Sonnet that creates paired honest vs deceptive instructions with consistent factual answers.Two complete 500-example JSONL datasets (Direct and Subtle deception), each covering 25 themes.A reproducible analysis pipeline (RunPod-friendly) that loads a base LLM (e.g. Llama 3.1 8B Instruct), extracts hidden states, and trains non-linear probes to detect deceptive intent from activations.What the pipeline doesGenerates high-quality deception-probing pairs using structured JSON outputs.Runs forward passes through the model with hidden-state extraction (residual stream).Builds pooled or per-token representation features for each example.Trains and evaluates non-linear MLP probes to classify honest vs deceptive intent.Compares intent signals across “Direct” (explicit harm) vs “Subtle” (manipulative, indirect) deception.Performs similarity analysis and representation-space comparisons across layers.Key resultsDirect deception yields very strong, easily separable activation signatures.Subtle deception is more challenging but still detectable significantly above chance.Early assistant-answer tokens already carry clear intent signals, even before the full answer is processed.

publications.title: A Novel Multimodal Deep Learning Framework for Generalizable Parkinson’s Disease Detection Using Handwriting and Speech
publications.subtitle: 48th Annual IEEE EMBC Conference
publications.description: Sole Author - Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor impairment and cognitive decline, making early detection critical for management. While prior deep learning studies successfully utilize speech or handwriting data to address this issue, they are constrained to single-modality, single-dataset, and single pattern settings due to the limited availability of handwriting and/or speech datasets catering to a specific pattern, and the complexity of multimodal learning and generalizing across patterns. We present a novel multimodal deep learning framework for Parkinson’s Disease (PD) detection using diverse handwriting and speech data to improve generalizability. We employ a multi-branch Neural Network (NN) architecture that processes handwriting and speech features separately before fusing for classification. Class imbalance is addressed using the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE). Results demonstrate a validation accuracy of 91%.

publications.title: A Simple Circuit for Time-Resolved Luminescence (TRL) Measurement Instruments: Demonstration Through a Smartphone-Based TRL Imager for Anticounterfeiting Application
publications.subtitle: IEEE Sensor Letters; Invited to present at IEEE Sensors@25
publications.description: Time-resolved luminescence (TRL) measurement is a sensitive detection technique by eliminating sample autofluorescence, but TRL measurement instruments composed of multiple key components (e.g., a rapidly pulsed light excitation source, a time-gated optical detector, and a synchronization module aligning the timing between the light source and the detector) have been sophisticated, expensive, or bulky, which limits their point-of-care or in-field applications. To reduce the cost and complexity of these instruments, in this letter, we developed a simple circuit for rapid LED pulsing and accurate timing synchronization and implemented it in a compact TRL imager with a ultraviolet light emitting diode (UV LED) as a light source and a chopper-coupled smartphone camera as a time-gated optical detector. The TRL measurement of this imager using this circuit was successfully validated through an anticounterfeiting application. We believe that this simple circuit can be adopted in the development of low-cost and compact TRL measurement instruments for broad point-of-care or in-field applications.

Accounting is so much more than the numbers: it's the language of business, with good reason. That was one of my biggest takeaways from the PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) Accounting Careers Leadership Institute, a selective five-day program that brought together 46 students from across the globe. Throughout the week, my perspective on this profession was rewired as I engaged in interactive sessions led by Bryant University College of Business professors in collaboration with PwC professionals in various specialties, from those who worked in audit to financial accounting. What we're often taught in school is accounting's role in a bookkeeping context, which doesn't grasp the magnitude of this career and just how transferrable it is to so many industries. Daily academic sessions covered accounting at the intersection of ethics, leadership, and the everchanging role of accountants in the age of AI. I enjoyed spending the week alongside my team (Ashley, Jonah, Charl, Roqué, and Sofia) under the guidance of our peer counselor Tianna-Lee Keovongvichit , with whom we worked through a variety of team-building activities like building a bike for charity, seeing group dynamics in action with a cup stacking challenge, and putting our minds together to construct a LEGO helicopter by taking turns looking at a reference model and reporting back to the group. At the culmination of the program, our team presented on the emerging importance of studying accounting, debunking common misconceptions about the career as well as highlighting its stability, immense potential, and applicability. Visiting PwC's Boston office was one of my favorite parts of the week. We got to hear insights from a panel of professionals working in audit and tax, hear perspectives about AI (which particularly captivated me in its potential to create agents tailored to specific tasks within the company), and see firsthand what a day in the life as an accountant looks like. Wanted to give a huge thank you to Bob Calabro and Tricia Benjamin , current PwC partners who were with us throughout the sessions to provide valuable anecdotes from their time with the firm as well as practical knowledge about the field as a whole. Lectures from Professor Charlie Cullinan were a highlight as he encouraged each of us to participate and work through real-world scenarios together. I also want to thank Ashley van Luling and Mailee Kue , who were the backbone of this program and helped provide us all with an amazing week of learning. #PwC #Accounting

🧠 The Two Physical Intelligence Tests — For World Models (Video attached below: 🎥 Left: Genesis simulation, 🎥 Right: Real physical experiment) At first glance, the simulation looks perfect — the motion is smooth, the timing feels natural, and everything seems physically correct. But when placed side by side with reality, the differences become obvious. This simple comparison raises a deeper question: What does it really mean for AI to understand the physical world? In my view, we can think of this as two Physical Intelligence Tests, each measuring a different level of understanding. 1️⃣ The First Physical Intelligence Test — The Illusion of Realism This test measures perception — how well AI satisfies what the human eye expects. A model passes when: 1) Humans can’t tell real from synthetic, or 2)The brain’s neural response (for example, in fMRI activation patterns) to both is indistinguishable. Many models already achieve this level of visual realism in simple settings. But looking plausible is not the same as being physically correct. 2️⃣ The Second Physical Intelligence Test — The Understanding of Physics The deeper test is causal: Can an AI model generate worlds that not only look real — but also obey the laws of physics? To pass, a model must internalize the causal logic of reality — forces, friction, boundary conditions — and sustain an internal imagination of motion that remains consistent with those laws over time. Hand-crafted physics simulation alone won’t get us there. Even today’s best numerical solvers break down in complex, real-world scenarios — fluid dynamics, deformable materials, granular motion. True physical intelligence must therefore be data-driven, learned and validated directly from how the real world behaves, not just how we approximate it. A physically intelligent model doesn’t just depict reality — it predicts and respects it. 3️⃣ Why It Matters — Closing the Sim2Real Gap Much of today’s hype around video world models comes from their promise to train embodied agents — letting AI learn to act, plan, and reason through simulated experience. But the Sim2Real gap — where systems work in simulation but fail in the real world — persists because most models stop at the first test. They optimize for appearances, not causes. A video can look perfect while quietly breaking physics underneath. That’s why agents trained in such synthetic worlds often fail when faced with real materials, friction, or uncertainty. Closing that gap requires models that pass the second Physical Intelligence Test — those whose internal reasoning aligns with the causal structure of reality. Only then can AI-generated worlds become reliable foundations for embodied intelligence and real-world reasoning. The first test measures perception. The second measures understanding. AI will bridge the Sim2Real gap not when it looks real — but when it behaves real. #ArtificialIntelligence #PhysicsAI #WorldModels #Sim2Real #EmbodiedIntelligence ...more ...more

Two weeks ago, I finally got the courage to record myself and post it on Instagram. For the past few months, I’ve been quietly working on Trajecta , an AI college consulting tool that helps students from 9-12th grade plan ahead for their college applications. I would put in hours every day adding new features, revising old UI, and testing output accuracy. But then something dawned on me. What do any of these iterations and continuous building even mean if nobody actually uses it? I’ve been avoiding the biggest and most uncomfortable part of creating a saas tool these days: marketing. And so a month ago, I decided to finally make some faceless content on TikTok. Most of the videos were funny videos related to colleges that only mentioned Trajecta at the very end of the video. These videos all performed very well, and after just four videos, I garnered over 500k+ views, and one of them even got reposted and went viral on X. Yet despite the traction, only around 20 people actually signed up to our website, and I became demotivated again and stopped posting. Two weeks ago, that changed. I finally decided to post videos with my face talking to the camera. I hate listening to my voice and videos of myself, but if I never got over the hump of posting and learning how to make content, my product would not get any trust, and I would just continue adding more features that no one would ever use. And it’s working. After just two weeks, I garnered over 300k views and 300+ followers, while my website finally got real paying users. I’m not posting every day yet. I’m not doing any fancy editing tricks. But I already broke through the toughest challenge I've faced these past few months. If you want to take a look at my new videos, go check out @yimingbuilds on Instagram. Still figuring things out, but more will be coming soon!

In 2004, Sal Khan 's 12-year-old cousin Nadia was placed into her school's slower math track. She told him, “I'm just not a math person.” Khan, a hedge fund analyst with 3 degrees from Massachusetts Institute of Technology , knew that one placement in middle school follows you for life. He made her a deal: if she'd give him half an hour a day after school, he'd tutor her over the phone and Yahoo Doodle. In the first two weeks, Nadia answered every math question with a question mark in her voice. "What's two to the third power?" She'd say, "Eight?" So Khan spent those sessions teaching her to say "eight" with confidence and conviction. Then he started teaching her math concepts ahead of her class, like negative exponents. When she understood them, he told her, "By the way, you're a 7th grader doing 10th grade math right now." She replied, "Really?" Khan called Nadia's school about retaking the placement exam. She moved from the remedial track to the advanced track. Word spread through the family. Soon Khan was tutoring 15 cousins across three time zones. A friend suggested he record the lessons for YouTube . Khan laughed: "YouTube is for cats playing piano, not for serious mathematics." He uploaded anyway. His entire studio was a walk-in closet, a $20 screen recorder, and Microsoft Paint. Viewers never saw his face, just heard a voice and watched equations fill the screen. Then Khan received a letter from a parent. Their 12-year-old son had autism, and every tutoring program they'd tried had failed him. Khan's recordings were the first resource that worked. Today, Khan Academy has nearly 190 million registered users. Nadia was taking university-level calculus by ninth grade. In a world where systems label us too early, conviction and support in another person's potential is the most underrated force. Be the person who offers it generously.

We’ve decided to open-source a multi-agent harness we use internally at YC. We call it “QM” and it’s meant to be easy to customize, like Hermes or OpenClaw, but useful for a whole company. We use it across accounting, legal, events, and engineering (including building QM itself!). The whole project is under an MIT license. It is cloud-first and has Slack and web UI natively. Some features: • Triggers (crons, webhooks), memory, shared files • Connectors for a company brain • Agent browser support • Shareable web app artifacts • Multi-player projects Like many things we do at YC, it’s an experiment. It’s early and has bugs. But it’s been surprisingly useful for us so far, and we’re excited to share it and get feedback from the community.
